Sal didn’t wait for the email, he walked down the hall to the caffeine abomination that took containers of what looked like ink and spat out a near-coffee substance. It was nearing four o’clock and this phone call meant he wasn’t going to be going home, or to sleep any time soon. When he read the email he had to set his coffee down. It was clear this was a real problem. He only hoped the data were enough to identify the compromised systems. He started with the traffic destination, and started scouring the proxy logs.

All traffic in and out of Calisto Drones International was forced through the proxy servers that Sal was responsible for. He pulled all logs he had, going back almost a year, and started grepping for event. He needed the thread, without the end of it he wouldn’t be able to follow it back to the beginning.

After about an hour of searching, he found it in an archive on the backup server. It was almost six months old.

Holy shit, how long have they been on our systems?

He took a breath, and started gathering more data. Two entries from the same source system inside the building, now three, a new source address…

Fuck, a lateral.

Without wasting any more time Sal picked up the phone and called Melinda, “Well Mel, we’re fucked.”

“What?” Sal could hear the exasperation over the phone, Melinda wasn’t known for her patience.

“Look, Intertron just called and sent me some compelling data. Apparently we’re hosting some pretty serious guests in our datacenter.” Sal was pretty well convinced, and a little highly strung by this point. But he took a breath and started to slow his tempo a bit.

“I’m on my way in, I’ll be there in about two hours.” Melinda had been on vacation and wasn’t due back until the next day.

“Mel, thanks. I need your help on this one.”

Sal hung up, and went back to hunting. He looked through every log he could find. He scoured every server he could knowing he was likely compromising his username and password every time he logged in to another system.

After another hour he turned off his monitor, stepped back and picked up a leather bound notebook. He opened it to an empty page and began writing.

gmeyer-desktop ssmith-desktop kthrace-desktop …

He sat staring at the list. This went on for another ten machines until he Mel walked in, tossed her backpack on her desk and threw herself into her chair.

“It’s big.” Sal said.

“What are we talking about?” Mel fired back as she logged in.

“At least a bakers dozen at first pass. Definitely more, I don’t have logs for all of the systems involved. I am having to make guesses based on kerberos event logs.”

Sal stood up and went to make another cup of coffee, Mark Sanders walked by him backpack in hand and greeted him with a nod. When he sat back down at his desk, cup of coffee in hand he pulled out the notebook and began describing the situation to Mark and Mel in detail.

Apparently the systems involved had been compromised by a user opening a PDF file that had contained malicious code. It sat in wait for a week using the AT command to schedule it’s next phase. It came to life and in a recursive turn of events used the at command to schedule another at command on another computer.

The at command essentially lets someone say “at this time do X to Y computer” and so it could be used as a proverbial time bomb once someone had taken advantage of a computer in a large network. Someone who was particularly motivated could even run amok like some sort of mad bomber setting timers on multiple systems to stay resident on the network.

The more Sal and Mel looked the more this became obvious. After about thirty minutes Mark came back with a cart full of workstations.

Nearly out of breath Mark announced, “That’s 9. At least four are left on that list.”

“We’ve found another 10, and likely even more. Here are the new ones.” Mel tore a page off of her notepad that she had just finished writing on.

And then it happened. They had been sloppy, they had tried to do it with three people and the unwanted guests had had over six months to prepare for this day.

The first sign anything bad was happening was when Sal tried to open Google and it was really slow to load.

“That’s funny.” Sal mentioned. A moment later he lost connection to a server he was logged in to. “Ok, that can’t be a coincidence.”

He started looking to see if there was something wrong but his logins weren’t working anywhere.

“Well you were right.” Mel said with none of her charactaristic sarcasm, “We’re fucked.”
